title: HTTP Debugging with curl
intro: curl is the universal HTTP debugger. A handful of flags let you reproduce almost any request a browser or service makes — and see what's really happening underneath.

steps.prompt: Call an authenticated API endpoint using a bearer token.
steps.explanation: -H adds a request header; here, the Authorization header most APIs expect.
steps.why: Keeping the token in a variable ($TOKEN) rather than pasting it keeps it out of your shell history and out of screenshots — tokens in bash history are a surprisingly common leak.

steps.prompt: Request http://example.com/docs and follow any redirects to the final page.
steps.fake_output:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://example.com/docs

HTTP/2 301
location: https://docs.example.com/

HTTP/2 200
steps.explanation: Two redirects: http → https, then to a docs subdomain.
steps.why: Without -L, curl stops at the first 301 and shows you a redirect page, which looks like 'the endpoint is broken'. -IL (headers only, follow) is the fastest way to map a whole redirect chain.

steps.prompt: Test one specific backend server (10.0.5.12) directly with the real hostname, bypassing DNS and the load balancer, to find which backend is misbehaving.
steps.explanation: --resolve forces curl to use 10.0.5.12 for api.example.com, while still sending the correct hostname for TLS (SNI) and the Host header.
steps.why: Just hitting https://10.0.5.12 directly would fail certificate validation (the cert is for the hostname, not the IP) and could route to the wrong virtual host. --resolve tests one backend exactly as real clients would reach it.

steps.prompt: See the full verbose exchange — request headers, response headers, and TLS handshake — for a failing request.
steps.fake_output:
* Connected to api.example.com (198.51.100.20) port 443
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3
> GET /orders HTTP/2
> Host: api.example.com
< HTTP/2 403
< x-amzn-waf-action: block
steps.explanation: The response header reveals a WAF (web application firewall) blocked the request — not the application.
steps.why: Response headers often identify which layer produced an error: a CDN, a WAF, a load balancer, or the app itself. Without -v you'd only see '403' and likely go debugging the wrong system.

steps.prompt: Break down where the time goes for a slow request: DNS, connect, TLS, and time to first byte.
expected_commands: curl -o /dev/null -s -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} connect:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n" https://api.example.com
steps.explanation: Network and TLS take 58ms combined; the server then takes ~2.75 seconds to produce the first byte.
steps.why: This pins slowness on the backend, not the network — so look at the app, its database queries, and its dependencies. Guessing 'the network is slow' without this breakdown wastes hours.
